answer_key_points: A PostgreSQL database cluster contains one or more named databases, and a database contains one or more named schemas, which in turn contain tables and other kinds of named objects, including data types, functions, and operators.

The same object name can be used in different schemas without conflict, and unlike databases, schemas are not rigidly separated: a user can access objects in any schema in the database they are connected to, if they have privileges to do so.
Within one schema, two objects of the same type cannot have the same name; tables, sequences, indexes, views, materialized views, and foreign tables share the same namespace.

answer_key_points: CREATE TABLE AS creates a table and fills it with data computed by a SELECT command; the table columns have the names and data types associated with the output columns of the SELECT, unless an explicit list of new column names overrides the column names.

It resembles creating a view but is quite different: it creates a new table and evaluates the query just once to fill the new table initially, so the new table will not track subsequent changes to the source tables of the query, whereas a view re-evaluates its defining SELECT statement whenever it is queried.
CREATE TABLE AS requires CREATE privilege on the schema used for the table.

answer_key_points: TRUNCATE acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on each table it operates on, which blocks all other concurrent operations on the table; if concurrent access is required, DELETE should be used instead.

TRUNCATE will not fire any ON DELETE triggers, but it will fire ON TRUNCATE triggers — all BEFORE TRUNCATE triggers fire before any truncation happens and AFTER TRUNCATE triggers fire after the last truncation and any sequence resets.

TRUNCATE is not MVCC-safe: after truncation, the table appears empty to concurrent transactions using a snapshot taken before the truncation occurred; however, it is transaction-safe and the truncation is rolled back if the surrounding transaction does not commit.

answer_key_points: When an object is created it is assigned an owner, and for most kinds of objects the initial state is that only the owner (or a superuser) can do anything with it, so privileges such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must be granted with the GRANT command to allow other roles to use it.

In addition to the SQL privilege system, tables can have row security policies that restrict, on a per-user basis, which rows can be returned by normal queries or modified by data modification commands; row security is enabled with ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.

When row security is enabled on a table, all normal access must be allowed by a row security policy, and if no policy exists a default-deny policy is used; operations that apply to the whole table, such as TRUNCATE and REFERENCES, are not subject to row security.
